\chapter{More of the Family}
\label{ch:sa-family-more}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a husband, a wife, a grandfather, a grandmother and a mother's brother in Sanskrit.}

Complete SA-C51-uncle and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[patiḥ]{\sk{पतिः} (patiḥ) — a husband}

\label{lesson:SA-C51-husband}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{ślokaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पतिः}}
\textbf{\sk{पतिः}} (\emph{patiḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a husband\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{पतिः}} is a husband, and more widely the master of a household.

It is one of the oldest words the family holds: Latin \emph{potis}, \textquotedblleft{}able, in command\textquotedblright{}, behind English \emph{possible} and \emph{power}, and Greek \emph{posis}, a husband. The \emph{-pati} that ends a great many Indian names and titles is this word doing the same work.

Beside \emph{kuṭumbam}, the household you can already name, \textbf{\sk{पतिः}} is the one who answers for it. Ends in \emph{-iḥ}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One end of a household, named.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{patiḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ślokaḥ}, then \emph{patiḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पतिः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a husband\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[patnī]{\sk{पत्नी} (patnī) — a wife}

\label{lesson:SA-C51-wife}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{patiḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पत्नी}}
\textbf{\sk{पत्नी}} (\emph{patnī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a wife\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{पत्नी}} is a wife, the mistress of the household.

It is \sk{पतिः} with a feminine ending laid on it, and the two have travelled together since before Sanskrit was Sanskrit: Greek \emph{potnia}, \textquotedblleft{}lady\textquotedblright{}, is the very same formation made in the very same way.

So the second word costs almost nothing once the first is yours. Feminine, ending in \emph{-ī}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pair that a household is built on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{patnī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{patiḥ}, then \emph{patnī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पत्नी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a wife\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pitāmahaḥ]{\sk{पितामहः} (pitāmahaḥ) — a grandfather}

\label{lesson:SA-C51-grandfather}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{patnī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पितामहः}}
\textbf{\sk{पितामहः}} (\emph{pitāmahaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a grandfather\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{पितामहः}} is a grandfather — and, precisely, the father's father.

Both halves are already yours. \sk{पिता} is the father, and \sk{महत्} is big; the ending shifts a little in the joining, but the sense does not. A grandfather is the great father.

Sanskrit keeps the two sides of a family apart, so this word does not stretch to the mother's side. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{अः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A new word made of two old ones.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pitāmahaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{patnī}, then \emph{pitāmahaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पितामहः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a grandfather\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mātāmahī]{\sk{मातामही} (mātāmahī) — a grandmother}

\label{lesson:SA-C51-grandmother}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{pitāmahaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मातामही}}
\textbf{\sk{मातामही}} (\emph{mātāmahī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a grandmother\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मातामही}} is a grandmother — and, precisely, the mother's mother.

It is built exactly as \sk{पितामहः} is, with \sk{माता} standing in front instead of \sk{पिता}. Having watched the joining once, you can read this one before it is explained.

The pair also shows the line Sanskrit draws down the middle of a family: one word for each side, and no word covering both. Feminine, ending in \emph{-ī}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The same joining, worked a second time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mātāmahī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pitāmahaḥ}, then \emph{mātāmahī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मातामही} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a grandmother\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mātulaḥ]{\sk{मातुलः} (mātulaḥ) — a mother's brother}

\label{lesson:SA-C51-uncle}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{pitāmahaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{mātāmahī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मातुलः}}
\textbf{\sk{मातुलः}} (\emph{mātulaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a mother's brother\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मातुलः}} is a mother's brother.

Sanskrit has no single word covering both uncles, and this is the one for the mother's side, with \sk{माता} standing plainly inside it. The line drawn by \sk{पितामहः} and \sk{मातामही} is drawn here too.

Latin drew it in the same place: \emph{avunculus} was the mother's brother, and it is the word English wore down into \emph{uncle}. Two languages, one distinction, one border apart. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{अः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five more of a household: a husband, a wife, a grandfather, a grandmother, a mother's brother.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mātulaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{patiḥ} and \emph{mātulaḥ} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मातुलः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a mother's brother\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
